strengths: Well-motivated and practically important problem (C-to-Rust translation for memory safety), with a sensible two-step methodology (unidiomatic-then-idiomatic) that separates semantic preservation from idiomaticity refinement.

The FFI-based end-to-end verification approach, which embeds translated Rust functions/harnesses back into the original C program to reuse existing tests, is a practical and scalable alternative to symbolic execution or fuzzing for verifying LLM-generated translations, and is clearly explained with concrete examples (Fig. 3).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning five LLMs (including a reasoning model, DeepSeek-R1), two curated datasets, and comparison against four existing baselines (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert) on both idiomaticity (Clippy alerts, unsafe fraction) and correctness (success rate) metrics.

Detailed, well-organized failure taxonomy (Tables 2–3, Figures 5–6) that breaks down error categories by model and dataset, offering actionable insight into current limitations of LLM-based translation (e.g., string handling, data type mismatches).

Cost analysis (tokens, query counts) across models adds a practical dimension often missing in similar papers, and the two real-world case studies (avl_tree, urlparser) provide an honest account of limitations when scaling beyond benchmark programs.
weaknesses: Relevance to ACL/computational linguistics is limited: the contribution is essentially a software-engineering tool/pipeline using LLMs as black-box translators, with no novel NLP or language-modeling technique, prompting methodology, or linguistic analysis; the paper reads more as an SE venue submission with LLMs as a component.

The "soft equivalence" verification approach depends entirely on the coverage and quality of end-to-end tests, which is not rigorously characterized (e.g., number/diversity of test cases per program, especially for Project CodeNet where SACTOR itself auto-generates the tests it later uses to validate its own translations, raising a circularity/bias concern).

The success-rate comparison against baselines (Table 5) is not clearly apples-to-apples: SACTOR is permitted up to 6 iterative feedback-guided attempts per translation, whereas rule-based baselines (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert) are one-shot/deterministic tools; this asymmetry is not discussed or controlled for.

Idiomaticity is measured almost entirely via automated Clippy lint counts and unsafe-code fraction, without any human judgment of readability, maintainability, or correctness of idiomatic constructs, which are the qualities the paper repeatedly emphasizes as important.

The real-world case studies are very limited in scope (only 2 projects) and reveal substantial partial failures (e.g., only 10/23 functions and 4/5 data types successfully translated to idiomatic Rust for urlparser), which weakens the generalizability claims beyond curated benchmark snippets.
No repeated-trial or variance analysis is reported despite LLM stochasticity (most models run at temperature 1), so the reported success rates and failure counts may not be robust point estimates.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the provided text (e.g., code/dataset URLs appear missing/placeholder), and some methodological specifics (e.g., how harness generation failures are distinguished from true translation failures) could be described more precisely.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem (C-to-Rust migration for memory safety) with a sensible two-phase design (unidiomatic-then-idiomatic) that explicitly separates the semantics-preservation concern from the idiomaticity-refinement concern.

The FFI-based end-to-end verification strategy, which links translated Rust back into the original C harness/test suite, is a reasonably practical alternative to symbolic execution or fuzzing baselines that the paper shows struggle with scalability, and is a genuinely useful engineering contribution.

Fairly broad empirical comparison across five LLMs (including a reasoning model) and against four existing C-to-Rust tools (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert), with idiomaticity measured via Clippy lint counts and unsafe-code fractions, giving a multi-faceted picture of translation quality.
Detailed failure-mode taxonomy (R1-R6, S1-S7) with per-model breakdowns adds diagnostic value beyond a single aggregate accuracy number.
Good transparency in reporting prompts (Appendix F), dataset construction/filtering criteria, and cost (token/query) accounting, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Weak evidence of real-world generalization: the two case studies (avl_tree, urlparser) — the only examples resembling realistic multi-function/multi-file C projects — show substantially degraded performance (e.g., only 10/23 functions and 4/5 data types translated idiomatically for urlparser; avl_bf never achieves idiomatic translation), which undercuts the headline 84-93% success rates obtained on the smaller, competitive-programming-style benchmark programs used for the main results.

The correctness notion ("soft equivalence" via passing existing/auto-generated end-to-end tests) is a materially weaker guarantee than claimed; for Project CodeNet the E2E tests are self-generated by the authors' own SACTOR test generator, creating a circularity risk where the same system both creates and evaluates its own oracle, and test coverage adequacy is not analyzed or discussed as a threat to validity.

Idiomaticity comparisons against baselines (Figure 7, Table 5) are computed only over programs each method successfully translates, but success rates differ substantially across methods (e.g., Vert 92% vs. SACTOR idiomatic 78-84%), so the comparison may suffer from survivorship bias rather than reflecting true relative quality on a matched sample.
No variance/repeated-run analysis is reported despite most LLMs being queried at temperature=1, making it unclear how stable the reported success rates and idiomaticity metrics are across runs.

The technical contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing components (C2Rust for types, Crown for pointer hints, iterative LLM prompting with compiler/test feedback) rather than a new modeling or NLP technique; there is limited discussion of what is conceptually novel beyond assembling known tools into a pipeline.

Relevance to the core ACL/NLP research agenda is thin: the paper does not propose new prompting, reasoning, or LLM-training techniques, nor does it study any linguistic or generation-quality phenomena specific to NLP; it reads as an applied software-engineering systems paper that happens to use off-the-shelf LLMs as a component, which may be a poor fit for the venue's scope.
The code/dataset availability footnote is left blank ("SACTOR code is available at" with no URL), undermining the stated reproducibility claims.

Some reported numbers are inconsistent across sections (e.g., abstract cites GPT-4o/Claude 3.5/DeepSeek-R1 all at 84% on one dataset while the conclusion states "GPT-4o reaching 80% correctness"), suggesting insufficient care in result reporting.

The idiomatic-phase verification approach fundamentally cannot handle certain common patterns (e.g., function pointers requiring FFI-compatible raw pointers vs. idiomatic generics, as shown in the avl_bf failure), and the paper does not propose or evaluate any mitigation, leaving an important class of real C code out of scope without a clear path forward.

strengths: Addresses a practical, well-motivated problem (translating legacy C to safe, idiomatic Rust) with a clearly articulated two-step methodology (unidiomatic-preserving translation followed by idiomatic refinement) that is intuitive and well explained.

Proposes a pragmatic and reasonably novel verification strategy: linking translated Rust code back into the original C program via FFI and running end-to-end tests, avoiding the scalability limitations of symbolic execution/fuzzing used in prior work (e.g., Vert).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning five LLMs (including a reasoning model, DeepSeek-R1), two curated datasets (200 programs total), and two real-world case studies, with multiple complementary metrics (success rate, Clippy lint counts, unsafe-code fraction, token/query cost).

Comparison against four existing baselines (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert) on idiomaticity and unsafe-code metrics, showing SACTOR's idiomatic phase achieves 100% unsafe-free code, a meaningful improvement.

Detailed, model-specific failure taxonomy (R1-R6, S1-S7) that offers useful diagnostic insight into where different LLMs struggle (e.g., string handling, data type mismatches), which is valuable for the community.
Sufficient methodological detail (including full prompts in the appendix) to support reproducibility attempts even absent public code release at review time.
weaknesses: The paper's core contribution is a software-engineering tool/pipeline; its connection to core NLP/computational linguistics contributions (e.g., novel LM techniques, linguistic analysis, benchmark for language understanding) is thin—the LLMs are used essentially off-the-shelf as translation engines, which may raise questions about fit for the ACL audience versus a software engineering venue.

The 'soft equivalence' verification relies entirely on the coverage and quality of available/generated end-to-end tests; for Project CodeNet, tests are auto-generated by the authors' own tool, and the paper does not quantify test coverage or discuss the risk that weak tests could pass despite functional divergence, undermining the correctness claims.

Datasets are drawn from competitive-programming/online-judge sources (TransCoder-IR, CodeNet), which are not representative of real, larger-scale legacy systems software that motivates the paper; the two real-world case studies are small (single projects) and show substantial partial failures (only 10/23 functions/4/5 types translated for urlparser), somewhat undercutting claims of broad real-world applicability.

No repeated-trial/variance analysis is reported despite LLM stochasticity (temperature=1 for most models); single-run success rates could be noisy, and confidence intervals or multiple seeds would strengthen the reliability of comparisons across models.

Idiomaticity is assessed only via Rust-Clippy warnings and unsafe-code fraction; there is no human/expert evaluation of readability or idiomatic quality, which are inherently more nuanced criteria than static lint counts.

Comparisons across baselines in Table 5/Figure 7 involve differing success rates and possibly different subsets of successfully translated programs across methods, raising concerns about whether idiomaticity metrics are computed on comparable (matched) program sets.

Potential data leakage/memorization concerns for well-known benchmark datasets (CodeNet, TransCoder-IR) that may appear in LLM pretraining corpora are not discussed, despite the paper's own criterion of avoiding datasets with paired Rust code specifically to mitigate this.
Reproducibility artifacts (code and dataset links) appear to be missing/placeholder in the manuscript, limiting immediate verifiability, though prompts and methodology are otherwise well documented.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem (converting legacy C to memory-safe, idiomatic Rust) with a well-motivated two-stage design (interface-preserving unidiomatic translation followed by idiomatic refinement) that cleanly separates semantic preservation from stylistic improvement.

Combines LLM generation with existing static-analysis tools (C2Rust for types, Crown for pointer ownership/fatness) and a novel FFI-based end-to-end verification scheme with a SPEC-driven harness generator (plus LLM fallback) to bridge ABI mismatches between unidiomatic and idiomatic Rust — a concrete and useful engineering contribution.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation: two curated benchmark datasets (200 programs), a 50-sample subset of CRust-Bench, and a real-world library (libogg); six LLMs including open-weight (Llama, DeepSeek) and closed models (GPT-4o/5, Claude, Gemini).

Extensive ablation studies (feedback mechanism, Crown's contribution, prompting strategies around 'unsafe', temperature sensitivity, trivial single-shot LLM baseline) that isolate the contribution of individual design choices rather than just reporting aggregate numbers.

Detailed, largely reproducible descriptions: task-division algorithm, SPEC schema, harness generation rules, LLM configurations, and full prompt templates are included in appendices, along with a thorough per-sample failure taxonomy for CRust-Bench and libogg.

Idiomaticity is measured with multiple concrete, tool-based metrics (Clippy lint counts, unsafe-code fraction, unsafe-free rate) and compared against several prior C-to-Rust baselines (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert), showing consistent improvements in safety/idiomaticity.
weaknesses: Relevance to the core scope of an NLP/CL venue is limited: the paper is essentially a software-engineering/program-transformation systems contribution that treats LLMs as an off-the-shelf component inside a pipeline; there is no new modeling, prompting theory, or linguistic/NLP analysis contributed beyond applying existing models with structured feedback.

Correctness is validated only via 'soft equivalence' against existing end-to-end test suites; the paper's own coverage numbers (e.g., 76–98% line/function coverage) and Limitations section acknowledge that shallow test coverage can mask semantic errors, which undercuts the strength of the 'correct' claim in the title, especially since deeper unit-level or property-based verification is not attempted.

On the more realistic and complex benchmarks (CRust-Bench, libogg), idiomatic-stage success rates are only moderate (43–78% depending on scope/model), and full-sample idiomatic success is much lower (8/32, 25%), indicating the method does not yet scale robustly to complex real-world pointer-heavy code — a caveat not fully reflected in the abstract's framing.

Idiomaticity evaluation relies solely on automated linting (Clippy) and unsafe-fraction metrics; there is no human or expert judgment of whether the produced Rust code is genuinely idiomatic (naming, abstraction quality, error handling elegance), which are the qualities the paper claims to optimize for.

Benchmark sizes remain modest (100 programs per dataset, 50/100 CRust-Bench samples, a single real-world library), limiting the strength of generalization claims across large-scale or highly heterogeneous C codebases.

Dependence on closed, versioned commercial APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0) raises reproducibility concerns, since these models can be deprecated or silently updated, and no discussion of potential data contamination (e.g., libogg or CRust-Bench code appearing in pretraining data) is provided.

The reported success-rate metrics mix multiple granularities (per-sample vs. per-function, averaged vs. aggregated, full-sample vs. partial) across tables, which, while thorough, makes the headline numbers somewhat difficult to compare and interpret consistently.

strengths: The system combines several established static-analysis tools (C2Rust for data-type translation, Crown for pointer/ownership analysis) with LLM-driven generation in a well-engineered two-stage pipeline (unidiomatic → idiomatic), which is a sensible decomposition of a genuinely hard problem.

The FFI-based end-to-end verification and the SPEC-driven harness-synthesis mechanism for bridging the ABI mismatch between C and idiomatic Rust is a non-trivial and useful technical contribution that goes beyond naive LLM prompting baselines.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: six LLMs, two general-purpose datasets (TransCoder-IR, CodeNet), and two more realistic targets (CRust-Bench subset, libogg), plus substantial ablations (feedback mechanism, Crown's contribution, unsafe-prompting variants, temperature, cost/token analysis).
Detailed, systematic failure-mode taxonomy and per-sample failure attribution (Appendices H, M) provide useful diagnostic insight rather than only aggregate numbers.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility material: prompts, algorithms, dataset preprocessing, and model configurations are all documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The paper's core contribution is primarily a software-engineering/verification pipeline (static analysis + FFI harness synthesis + compiler/test feedback loops) in which the LLM is used largely as an interchangeable black-box generator; there is little study of linguistic/generation behavior, prompting science, or NLP-specific insight that would anchor this as a computational-linguistics contribution rather than an SE/PL systems paper, raising doubts about fit and relevance for an ACL venue.

Correctness claims rest on "soft equivalence" via existing (or auto-generated) end-to-end tests whose coverage varies substantially across datasets (e.g., CodeNet tests are synthetically generated, CRust-Bench/libogg coverage is 75-83% line/function per Table 5); this undermines confidence that passing tests implies true semantic equivalence, a point the authors themselves flag as a limitation.

On the two more realistic, repository-scale benchmarks that best approximate real-world utility, idiomatic-stage success is modest (52% on CRust-Bench, 53-78% on libogg) and unidiomatic-to-idiomatic translation is only evaluated on the subset of samples that fully succeeded at the unidiomatic stage, which likely overstates effective end-to-end success on a full codebase.

Idiomaticity is assessed only via Clippy lint counts and unsafe-code fraction; no human judgment or qualitative assessment of whether "idiomatic" Rust is actually idiomatic/maintainable is provided, despite idiomaticity being a central claim of the paper.

Baseline comparisons (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert) are run only with GPT-4o for the LLM-based ones, and SACTOR's own showcased results often rely on DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-5, making head-to-head idiomaticity/correctness comparisons somewhat uneven across the reported tables.

Reliance on closed, versioned proprietary APIs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0) and a non-deterministic feedback/retry loop limits long-term reproducibility, since these model endpoints can be deprecated or silently updated.

The sheer volume of appendix material (35 pages of ablations, failure tables, and prompts) suggests the evaluation is sprawling rather than tightly synthesized into a small number of clear, well-supported claims, making it hard to assess which findings are most load-bearing for the paper's contribution.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning two synthetic benchmarks (TransCoder-IR, CodeNet) and two realistic targets (CRust-Bench subset, libogg), across six different LLMs, giving a fairly thorough picture of the method's behavior under varying conditions.

The two-stage design (interface-preserving unidiomatic translation followed by idiomatic refinement) is a sensible decomposition that separates syntactic/semantic concerns from idiomatic style concerns, and is empirically shown to matter (e.g., ablation against a one-shot baseline in Appendix J.2 shows large gains from decomposition).

The FFI-based verification approach, including the SPEC-driven harness synthesis to bridge ABI mismatches between C and idiomatic Rust, is a practical and non-trivial engineering contribution that addresses a genuine gap (prior tools like Vert/Flourine rely on impractical fuzzing/symbolic execution or don't verify idiomatic output at all).

Extensive ablation studies (feedback mechanism, Crown's contribution, unsafe-prompting variants, temperature sensitivity) substantiate specific design choices rather than just reporting end results, and the Crown ablation (Appendix J.3) offers a compelling information-theoretic argument for why static analysis hints are necessary.
Detailed, well-organized failure taxonomy (Appendix H, M) with per-sample breakdown for CRust-Bench, which supports transparency and aids reproducibility/diagnosis of the tool's limitations.
Reasonable transparency about limitations (test-coverage dependence, unsupported C features, harness fragility, cost) in a dedicated Limitations section.
Reproducibility artifacts (prompts, LLM configurations, dataset preprocessing details) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The correctness guarantee is only as strong as the existing E2E test suites used ("soft equivalence"); coverage numbers (e.g., 76-98% line coverage) suggest meaningful gaps remain in verifying semantic correctness, and this is a fundamental limitation of the central correctness claim rather than a minor caveat.

On the more realistic benchmark (CRust-Bench), idiomatic success is modest (52% per-sample average, only 8/32 fully idiomatic), and many failure categories (name drift, borrow-checker violations, harness faults) suggest the method is still fairly fragile outside curated benchmarks; scalability to larger/more complex real-world codebases remains unproven beyond one library (libogg).

Baseline comparisons (C2Rust, Crown, C2SaferRust, Vert) are only performed on the two synthetic datasets and only with GPT-4o as the LLM backbone for SACTOR in that comparison; there is no comparison against these baselines on CRust-Bench or libogg, making it harder to assess whether SACTOR's advantage generalizes to more complex, realistic code.

Unsupported C features (variadics, function pointers, complex macros, inline assembly, circular dependencies) are excluded from evaluation by design (e.g., CRust-Bench subset explicitly filters these), which may inflate apparent success rates relative to what would be seen on arbitrary real-world C code.

No variance/statistical significance is reported despite running translations multiple times (e.g., "up to three times per sample" for real-world codebases); given LLM stochasticity, some measure of run-to-run variability would strengthen the empirical claims.

The individual technical components (C2Rust for types, Crown for pointer semantics, LLM-based translation with compiler feedback) are each pre-existing; the primary novelty is in the orchestration/pipeline and the SPEC-driven harness verification, which is a valid but comparatively incremental combination of known techniques.

Cost trade-offs (DeepSeek-R1 using 5-7x more tokens than GPT-4o) are documented but not analyzed in terms of practical deployment recommendations, leaving unclear guidance on when the accuracy/idiomaticity gains justify the added cost.
